title: The Righteous Are Bold as a Lion
summary: This chapter contrasts the wicked and the righteous in public life, especially in how rulers treat the poor. It praises those who keep God's law, commends integrity over wealth, and warns against greed, partiality, and flattery. At its center is one of the Bible's clearest sayings on confession: the one who conceals sin will not prosper, but the one who confesses and renounces it will find mercy.
story: Chapter 28 continues the Hezekiah collection, and it has a distinct flavor. More than any other part of Proverbs, it speaks of the law (torah), and it repeatedly considers what happens to a people when the wicked or the righteous hold power. The collection seems to have been shaped with rulers and future rulers in mind, which fits its preservation by scribes of the royal court. Yet the sayings reach everyone: the poor man with integrity, the son who keeps the law, the man hiding his sin.
historical:
Several sayings reflect political instability. Verse 2 notes that a land in rebellion has many rulers. Israel knew this well: the northern kingdom had a series of short-lived dynasties, with kings assassinated and replaced repeatedly in its last decades before Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC. For readers in Hezekiah's Judah (about 715 to 686 BC), who had watched that collapse from nearby, the proverb was no abstraction. A man of understanding, by contrast, brings stability.

Verse 8 addresses lending at interest. The law of Moses forbade Israelites to charge interest to a fellow Israelite in need (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35-37; Deuteronomy 23:19-20). Moneylending at high rates was common across the ancient Near East, and it often drove poor farmers into debt slavery. The proverb says that wealth gained this way will end up with someone who is kind to the poor.
cultural:
The poor in ancient Israel were mostly small farmers vulnerable to drought, debt, and the greed of powerful neighbors or officials. The prophets of the eighth century BC, such as Amos, Micah, and Isaiah, condemned the seizure of fields and the corruption of courts in terms that match this chapter. Verse 3 pictures a ruler who is himself needy and oppresses the poor, like a driving rain that washes the crops away instead of watering them; some interpreters read the Hebrew as a poor man who oppresses the poor.

Rebuke and flattery were matters of public life, especially in a royal court. Verse 23 praises the one willing to rebuke, even if he is not thanked at first. Verse 24 condemns a son who robs his parents and says it is no crime, likely by taking the family inheritance early or failing to support aging parents, and Jesus condemned a related evasion of the duty to support parents in the religious teaching of his day (Mark 7:9-13).
literary: The chapter is built mainly of antithetical proverbs, in which the second line states the opposite of the first, usually contrasting the righteous and the wicked. Verses 12 and 28 frame much of the chapter with a pair of similar sayings about what happens when the wicked rise and when they fall: people hide themselves. The word torah (law or instruction) appears in verses 4, 7, and 9, and the word poor appears repeatedly. Verses 6 and 18 both speak of walking with integrity, a picture of life as a path. Verse 13 stands out as a direct statement about confession, rare in its explicitness among the proverbs.

outline.t: Bold righteousness, ruling well, and keeping the law
Wicked rulers and the path of integrity
Trusting the LORD, giving to the poor

doctrines.note: Verse 13 describes repentance in two movements: confessing sin and renouncing it. Concealment leads to ruin, but the one who does both finds mercy. This is one of the Old Testament's clearest statements that God meets confession with compassion.

Keeping the law is linked with wisdom, discernment, and resisting the wicked (verses 4, 7, 9). Proverbs doesn't usually speak in terms of Moses' law, so this chapter shows that wisdom and law were understood as partners, not rivals.
The chapter judges rulers by how they treat the poor and whether they hate dishonest gain (verses 3, 15, 16). God's standard for government is justice for the weak, not power for its own sake.

words.note: Torah, law or instruction. The word can mean a parent's or teacher's instruction, as often in Proverbs, or God's law given through Moses. In this chapter the phrases keep the law and forsake the law point toward God's revealed instruction, and verse 9 warns that turning away from it makes even prayer detestable.

Kasah, to cover or conceal. In verse 13 the one who covers his sins will not prosper. The same verb is used elsewhere of God covering sin in forgiveness (Psalm 32:1). The difference is who does the covering: human concealment brings ruin, while God's covering brings pardon.

Racham, to have compassion or show mercy, related to the word for womb. Verse 13 says the one who confesses and renounces sin will find mercy. The word evokes tender, parental compassion, the kind God shows to his people.

Batach, to trust. It appears three times in the chapter. The righteous are bold, literally confident, as a lion (verse 1); the one who trusts in the LORD will prosper (verse 25); but the one who trusts in himself is a fool (verse 26). Proverbs asks not whether we trust, but in whom.

christ: Verse 13 anticipates the New Testament promise that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9). The chapter's picture of the righteous ruler who hates dishonest gain and protects the poor describes a king Israel rarely had, and the prophets looked forward to a son of David who would judge the poor with righteousness. Christians see that king in Jesus, who proclaimed good news to the poor, who did not flatter but told the truth in love, and whose kingdom turns the wicked ruler's pattern upside down. These are links of theme and hope, not direct predictions.

hard.q: Verse 27 says whoever gives to the poor will not be in need. Is that a promise that generosity always pays?
hard.a: Read this way, verse 27 would become a kind of prosperity formula: give, and you will never lack. But it is a proverb, and proverbs describe how life usually goes under God, not a guarantee for every case. Generous people tend to live in communities where they are known and helped in their own need, and God delights to care for those who care for others. Yet the Bible is full of generous, faithful people who were poor, and the New Testament praises a widow who gave all she had. The same chapter says a poor man who walks with integrity is better than a rich man (verse 6), which shows that Proverbs does not measure faithfulness by wealth. The verse's point is that giving is not a loss in God's economy, and that the one who hides his eyes from the poor stores up curses instead.

questions: Verse 13 contrasts concealing and confessing sin. What makes confession so hard, and what has your experience been when you have done it?
Verse 1 says the wicked flee when no one pursues. How does a guilty conscience shape a person's life?
The chapter judges leaders by how they treat the poor. How would that standard change the way you evaluate leaders you know, including yourself?
